This paper proposes Grouped Head Attention (GHA), a training strategy for multi-head attention that explicitly groups heads into clusters via a self-supervised constraint, encouraging intra-group similarity and inter-group diversity, followed by a Voting-to-Stay pruning procedure that retains one representative “pillar of strength” head per group. The paper argues that this divide-and-conquer approach addresses both redundancy and over-parameterization in MHA better than prior homogenization-only, diversification-only, or significance-based pruning methods. Empirically, the method is evaluated on machine translation, abstractive summarization, and language modeling, with reported gains over vanilla Transformers and several efficiency-oriented baselines, while also reducing parameters and FLOPs after pruning.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and reasonably well-motivated. The central intuition—that useful head structure may lie between full diversity and full homogenization, and that one can first induce grouped specialization and then prune within groups—is appealing. The empirical scope is also broader than many head-pruning papers, spanning three NLP tasks rather than only MT. The reported results are strong, and the ablations suggest that both the grouping constraint and the pruning stage matter. At the same time, I have several concerns about methodological clarity, fairness of comparison, and the strength of the causal claims made from the experiments. My assessment is that the paper has merit, but some of its conclusions are stronger than what is fully supported by the current presentation.

The main strength of the paper is the conceptual framing. Prior work often treats head redundancy either by encouraging diversity across all heads or by pruning heads deemed unimportant after training. This work instead proposes a structured intermediate regime: heads are partitioned into groups, heads within a group are intentionally made similar, and groups are pushed apart. This is a sensible idea because it creates redundancy that is organized rather than accidental, making subsequent pruning more principled. The two-stage design is coherent, and the “group then prune” logic is easy to understand. I also appreciate that the paper attempts to connect the method to measurable notions of compactness and cluster quality, rather than only reporting end-task metrics.

Another strength is the breadth of empirical evaluation. The paper reports results on multiple MT datasets, CNN/DailyMail summarization, and WikiText-103 language modeling. This is valuable because many architectural efficiency papers overfit their narrative to a single benchmark. The ablation study on MT is also useful: removing the homogenization term, diversification term, GCT, or the PS selection mechanism all hurts performance, which supports the claim that the full method matters. The analysis of group compactness versus BLEU is also suggestive and helps motivate the claim that there is an optimal degree of grouping pressure.

That said, my biggest concern is that the method description is not sufficiently precise for a top-tier ML venue. Several components remain underspecified or somewhat ad hoc. The Hidden Unit Discovery System is described abstractly as an unsupervised clustering algorithm, with K-means used in experiments, but it is unclear exactly when clustering is run during training, on what representations, with what normalization, and at what computational cost. Since the cluster assignments supervise the model while the model simultaneously changes the feature maps being clustered, the optimization procedure is effectively alternating between representation learning and clustering. This can be unstable, and the paper does not clearly explain the schedule, convergence behavior, or sensitivity to initialization. The convergence criterion for V2S depends on cluster center shift being below a threshold, but the threshold and practical robustness are not clearly discussed in the main text.

Relatedly, the formulation of the loss in Eq. (4) is difficult to parse and raises questions. The paper says it uses the metric-learning version in experiments, but the exact architecture used to compare feature maps and hidden units is not fully specified. Since the value maps, attention maps, and output maps have different shapes and semantics, it is not obvious how cosine similarity is computed consistently across them without additional projections or pooling. The text mentions that metric learning avoids extra projection layers “when the shapes of similarity inputs are identical,” but in practice these feature maps are not naturally identical in shape. This is an important implementation detail because the claimed parameter efficiency of GHT depends on not adding substantial auxiliary machinery. The paper would benefit from a much clearer explanation of how each feature map is transformed before clustering and before similarity computation.

A second major concern is fairness and consistency of the baselines. Some comparisons are convincing, but others are less so. For example, GHT is compared to vanilla Transformer at equal parameter count, which is fair. GHT-PS is compared to reduced-capacity Transformer variants and pruning baselines at roughly equal parameter count, which is also reasonable. However, some of the stronger claims compare across architectures, training recipes, and parameter scales in ways that are not fully controlled. In the language modeling section, the paper compares against models such as GPT-2 Large, BERT-L-CAS, and S4, but these are not matched in training data, optimization setup, or even modeling assumptions. Such comparisons are not very informative unless carefully normalized. The strongest evidence is really the comparison to the backbone transformer with adaptive input; the broader SOTA comparison should be framed more cautiously.

Similarly, in summarization, the comparison includes older convolutional and recurrent baselines, which are less relevant than stronger modern Transformer-based summarization systems. Since the paper’s contribution is specifically about MHA efficiency and redundancy, the most compelling baselines would be recent attention-efficient or pruning-based Transformer summarizers under matched training conditions. The current table shows gains, but it does not fully establish state-of-the-art standing in a rigorous sense.

A third concern is that the paper’s interpretation of why the method works is plausible but not conclusively demonstrated. The authors argue that GCT causes each group to focus on an “essential but distinctive feature subset,” and that the retained PS head preserves the essential utility of the group. However, the evidence provided is mostly indirect: improved task performance, cluster compactness metrics, and ablations. There is little direct analysis showing that grouped heads indeed attend to semantically distinct phenomena or that the PS head functionally subsumes the others in its group. For a paper centered on head structure, I would have liked to see qualitative or quantitative analyses of attention behavior, such as similarity of attention patterns within groups, specialization across syntactic or positional roles, or probing of retained versus removed heads. Without such evidence, the “pillar of strength” terminology feels somewhat stronger than warranted.

There is also a possible confound in the reported gains: the grouping loss may simply act as a regularizer that improves optimization, rather than specifically discovering a better structural decomposition of heads. The ablations partly address this, but not fully. For instance, comparing against other regularization strategies with similar strength, or against simpler structured head-sharing/grouping baselines, would help isolate whether the benefit comes from the proposed clustering-based supervision specifically. As written, it remains possible that much of the gain is due to auxiliary regularization rather than the particular group-discovery mechanism.

The computational overhead during training is another under-discussed issue. The paper emphasizes inference efficiency after pruning, but GCT appears to require extracting multiple feature maps from every head and periodically clustering them. V2S also requires a voting epoch over the training set with the model frozen. These costs may be acceptable, but they should be quantified. For an efficiency paper, reporting only inference speed and FLOPs while omitting training-time overhead is incomplete. If the method substantially increases training cost or implementation complexity, that affects its practical value. At minimum, the paper should report wall-clock training time relative to the backbone and clarify how often clustering is performed.

I also have some concerns about the statistical reporting and presentation of results. The paper repeatedly reports percentage improvements in BLEU, ROUGE, or perplexity, but it is not always clear whether these are relative or absolute improvements, and relative percentages on metrics like BLEU can be misleading. Absolute gains should be emphasized. The use of t-tests is mentioned, but the number of runs and variance estimates are not clearly presented in the main text. For neural sequence models, significance claims are much more convincing when accompanied by mean and standard deviation over multiple seeds. Some tables appear to report single numbers only. Given that several gains are modest in absolute terms, variance reporting is important.

There are also some technical and writing issues. The paper has a number of grammatical errors and awkward phrasings, and some notation is inconsistent or overloaded. For example, the indexing in the clustering objective and hidden-unit notation is occasionally confusing. The algorithm description for V2S is high-level and omits practical details needed for reproduction. The paper also sometimes overstates novelty or certainty, for example by claiming to “verify” the hypothesis that compactness improves performance, whereas the evidence is correlational and limited to a small number of runs on development sets. These issues do not invalidate the contribution, but they reduce clarity and rigor.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has several genuinely valuable aspects. The idea of inducing structured redundancy before pruning is novel enough relative to prior head-pruning and head-diversification work. The empirical results, especially on MT against matched-capacity baselines, are promising. The ablations are directionally supportive. If the method is as simple and robust as the paper suggests, it could be useful in practice and may inspire follow-up work on structured head organization.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following. First, clarify the training algorithm in detail: when clustering is run, how feature maps are pooled/projected, how hidden units are represented in the metric-learning version, and what the training overhead is. Second, add stronger controlled baselines, especially simpler grouping or regularization alternatives, to isolate the contribution of the proposed mechanism. Third, report multi-seed means and standard deviations for the main results. Fourth, include direct analyses of grouped head behavior and PS-head representativeness, rather than relying mainly on end-task metrics and cluster compactness scores. Fifth, moderate some of the broader claims about discovering essential feature subsets unless supported by more direct evidence.

In summary, this is a thoughtful and potentially impactful paper with a nice core idea and encouraging empirical results, but it falls short of full rigor in methodological specification and causal validation. I view it as a solid contribution with meaningful promise, especially if the authors can better justify the mechanism, quantify training overhead, and tighten the experimental comparisons. My overall recommendation would be cautiously positive if the venue values practical architectural ideas with broad empirical validation, but I would want the above concerns addressed for a strong acceptance case.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Grouped Head Attention (GHA), a modification/training strategy for multi-head attention that clusters heads into groups using self-supervised hidden units derived from head feature maps. Training uses a group-constrained objective to encourage intra-group similarity and inter-group diversity, after which a Voting-to-Stay (V2S) pruning procedure retains one representative head per group to form a compressed model (GHT-PS). Experiments on machine translation, abstractive summarization, and language modeling report improved accuracy and efficiency relative to vanilla Transformers and several prior head-reduction baselines.
strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: redundancy and over-parameterization in multi-head attention.
The proposed approach combines diversity encouragement and pruning in a unified framework, which is conceptually more comprehensive than methods that only diversify or only prune.
Empirical evaluation spans three NLP tasks (MT, summarization, LM), suggesting some breadth of applicability.
Includes ablations on major components (homogenization/diversification, GCT, HUDS, PS selection) and analysis of group number and compactness trends.
Reports efficiency metrics beyond accuracy, including parameter count, FLOPs, and inference speed.
weaknesses: The method description is often unclear and mathematically under-specified, making it difficult to verify correctness or reproduce the approach precisely.

The central grouping mechanism relies on non-differentiable clustering (e.g., K-means) over evolving head feature maps, but the interaction between clustering updates and gradient-based training is not rigorously defined.
The claimed scientific insight that greater group compactness improves performance is supported only by correlational plots over a few runs, not by controlled causal evidence.

Comparisons to baselines are not always fully fair: some baselines differ substantially in architecture, scale, or training recipe, and the paper does not clearly establish matched hyperparameter tuning budgets.
Statistical significance claims via t-tests are weakly supported because the number of runs is not consistently specified and variance reporting is largely absent.
The pruning rule keeps one head per group by design, which may be overly restrictive and may confound whether gains come from grouping regularization, pruning, or simply altered capacity allocation.
The paper overstates generality; all experiments are on NLP and mostly on moderate-scale settings rather than modern large pretrained transformers.
methodological_flaws: Equation (3) is presented as the clustering objective for hidden-unit discovery, but the notation is inconsistent: the outer sum index runs over groups while the text alternates between head groups and feature-map groups, and the optimization variable Z is treated both as assignments and hidden units. This makes the mathematical object being optimized ambiguous.

Equation (4) is not rigorously justified. In the categorical case, the second term maximizes log-probability of other-group hidden units conditioned on a head's feature maps, which appears counterintuitive for diversification; if the intent is repulsion, the sign/interpretation is unclear. In the continuous case, the loss mixes cosine similarities between heterogeneous objects (value maps, attention maps, output maps, and hidden units) without specifying dimensional alignment or normalization details.

The training procedure depends on hidden units discovered by an unsupervised algorithm over model activations, but the paper does not specify update frequency, stability mechanisms, or convergence guarantees. Since clustering assignments can change discontinuously during training, optimization may be unstable; this is not analyzed.

The V2S score definition appears inconsistent: for continuous hidden units, the representative head score is defined as negative cosine similarity to its assigned hidden unit, which would favor less similar heads unless there is an omitted sign convention. This is a potential logic error in the pruning criterion.

The convergence condition for triggering V2S ('center shift less than a threshold') is not operationally specified, and sensitivity to this threshold is not studied. This undermines reproducibility and empirical validity.

Claims of causal benefit from 'compactness' are not established. Figure-based evidence uses only a handful of runs on dev sets and tunes alpha/beta, but does not disentangle whether compactness itself or regularization strength/hyperparameter choice drives performance.

Efficiency claims are somewhat overstated because masking heads during training is not equivalent to actual structured pruning, and real implementation details for speedups are not sufficiently documented. Reported inference gains are modest in some tables and may depend heavily on implementation.

Empirical comparisons to prior work may be confounded by differing backbones and training setups. For example, some baselines are older or architecturally different, and there is limited evidence that each baseline was reimplemented and tuned under identical conditions.

The paper invokes the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis as explanatory support, but no actual lottery-ticket-style experiment (rewinding, sparse subnetwork identification, matching initialization) is conducted; this is speculative rather than validated scientific reasoning.
